statement_en: Is there a function $f(n)$ and a $k$ such that in any $k$-colouring of the integers there exists a sequence $a_1<\cdots$ such that $a_n<f(n)$ for infinitely many $n$ and the set\[\left\{ \sum_{i\in S}a_i : \textrm{finite }S\right\}\]does not contain all colours?
statement_lean:
theorem erdos_32262 :
    ∃ (f : ℕ → ℕ) (k : ℕ), 0 < k ∧ ∀ colouring : ℤ → Fin k,
      ∃ a : ℕ → ℤ, StrictMono a ∧ {n | a n < f n}.Infinite ∧
        ∃ c : Fin k, ∀ S : Finset ℕ, S.Nonempty → colouring (∑ i ∈ S, a i) ≠ c := by
  sorry

issues: Domain mismatch. In the Hindman-type setting of A (Erdős's usage), 'the integers' almost certainly means positive integers, and a_1<a_2<... is a sequence of positive integers. B instead quantifies over colourings of all of ℤ and explicitly allows the sequence to take negative values. That changes both the class of colourings and the class of admissible sequences.

A proof of B does not transfer to the positive-integer version. Extending an ℕ-colouring to ℤ and applying B may produce a sequence with negative terms, whose finite sums include non-positive integers that lie outside the original colouring's domain.

Allowing negative terms gives the prover extra freedom. For example, a very negative a_0 shifts half of all subset sums into a region the colouring may treat differently, so B may be strictly weaker than the intended claim.

Empty sum. B restricts to nonempty finite S. Under a literal reading of A with the empty sum included, the colour of 0 is always present, so A would require a missing colour other than the colour of 0. B lets the missing colour c equal the colour of 0, which is a weakening. The nonempty reading is the standard Hindman convention, so this is minor.
Minor differences that do not matter: B indexes from a_0 instead of a_1 (absorbed by the free choice of f), and B requires k to be positive.
faithfulness.verdict: B works over ℤ-colourings and allows sequences with negative terms. It is therefore at best a weakened variant of the intended positive-integer Hindman-type question, and a proof of B would not legitimately settle A in the positive direction.
faithfulness.backtranslation: There exist a function f from the natural numbers to the natural numbers and a positive integer k with the following property. For every colouring of the integers with k colours, there is a strictly increasing sequence of integers a₀ < a₁ < a₂ < ⋯ (which may take negative values) and a colour c such that two conditions hold. First, aₙ < f(n) for infinitely many n. Second, no sum ∑_{i∈S} aᵢ over a finite nonempty set S of indices receives colour c.
